wu: Two Truths and a Lie: Students write three life experiences (e.g., 'I have visited Paris,' 'I have never eaten sushi,' 'I have met a celebrity'). In pairs, they guess which is the lie. Teacher models first: 'I have climbed Mount Toubkal, I have never been to America, I have won a poetry prize.'
wuAlt: Find Someone Who: Students mingle asking 'Have you ever...?' questions (e.g., 'Have you ever tried Moroccan mint tea?', 'Have you ever traveled abroad?'). They write names next to true statements.
Experience Bingo: Teacher calls out experiences (e.g., 'Have you ever broken a bone?', 'Have you ever missed a flight'). Students mark their bingo cards if true.
pres: Teacher shows a photo of a haunted house and asks: 'Have you ever been to a haunted house?' Elicits model sentences: 'Yes, I have. I went last year.' vs 'No, I haven't. I've never been to one.' Highlights 'have/has + past participle' and 'ever/never'. Checks understanding with thumbs up/down for true/false sentences (e.g., 'She has never tried pumpkin pie').
presAlt: Timeline Story: Teacher draws a timeline on the board (childhood, teens, now). Adds events with both tenses: 'When I was 10, I broke my arm (past simple). I have never broken a bone since (present perfect).' Students ask questions.

Picture Comparison: Two photos (one of a child, one of an adult). Teacher says: 'As a child, I loved Halloween. Now, I have never celebrated it.' Students compare their own past and present experiences.
prac: Tense Toss: Students stand in a circle. Teacher tosses a soft ball and says a sentence (e.g., 'I have eaten couscous'). Student catches it and changes it to past simple (e.g., 'I ate couscous last week') or asks a question (e.g., 'Have you ever eaten tagine?').
pracAlt: Sentence Race: Two teams race to write correct sentences on the board. Teacher says a prompt (e.g., 'never/see/snow'). Teams write: 'I have never seen snow.'
Interview Relay: In pairs, Student A asks 'Have you ever...?' questions. Student B answers with present perfect, then asks a follow-up past simple question (e.g., 'When did you go?'). Swap roles.
ls: Listen to a short interview about Halloween traditions. Students tick experiences mentioned (e.g., 'carved a pumpkin', 'dressed up', 'trick-or-treated'). Then, in pairs, they discuss: 'Which have you done? Which haven't you?'
re: Experience Charades: One student mimes an experience (e.g., riding a camel). Others guess: 'Have you ever ridden a camel?' The mimer responds: 'Yes, I have. I did it last summer.'
prod: Halloween Debate: Two teams (Team Commerce: 'Halloween is just a business opportunity.' Team Culture: 'Halloween enriches traditions'). Each team has 2 minutes to present, then 1 minute for rebuttals. Teacher monitors for present perfect/past simple use (e.g., 'We have seen shops sell more decorations' vs 'Last year, we didn't celebrate it').
rw: Read a short article about Halloween in Morocco. Underline all present perfect sentences. Then, write 4 sentences comparing Halloween to a Moroccan celebration (e.g., 'Many Moroccans have never celebrated Halloween, but they have always enjoyed Eid al-Fitr').
st: Read a short ghost story from Morocco (e.g., 'The Jinn of the Old Medina'). Discuss: 'Have you ever heard a story like this?' End with: 'Today, we compared experiences using present perfect and past simple. Thank you, class.'
g: Students toss a ball and change present perfect to past simple or ask a question.
Students mingle asking 'Have you ever...?' questions and write names.
Students mime experiences; others guess using present perfect questions.
Teams race to write correct present perfect/past simple sentences.
Pairs ask/answer questions using both tenses.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a paragraph comparing Halloween to Green March or Independence Day.
Support: Use a sentence frame: 'I have never ___. Last year, I ___ instead.'
hw: Summarise a real article about life experiences in 4 sentences (e.g., from a Moroccan news website).
Write a short opinion paragraph: 'Should Oujda celebrate Halloween? Use present perfect and past simple.'
Interview a family member about their past experiences and write 3 questions/answers using both tenses.
tip: Emphasize the cultural context: Compare Halloween to local festivals like Green March to make grammar relevant. Use students' real experiences to boost engagement.
